title: The manners, reviewed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart, and your line: check the heart. One list for what grows, one for what makes it sick. Did you take the checkup before sleep? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

A boy sits at a shared platter of food in the Prophet's house. He is the stepson of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he is hungry, and his hand is everywhere: this side of the dish, that side, wherever the best piece seems to be. The Prophet speaks to him with three short instructions. Say the name of Allah. Eat with your right hand. Eat from what is in front of you. That's all. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the boy, Umar ibn Abi Salamah, remembers it, and says, in paraphrase, that this stayed his way of eating from then on. Today, the manners again: adab in everything.
screen: `A HAND ALL OVER THE PLATTER.` → `THREE SHORT INSTRUCTIONS.` → `IT STAYED HIS WAY OF EATING.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Adab, as the year defined it, is courtesy: toward Allah, toward people, and toward things. Not etiquette for show, but the shape a faith takes in small moments. Second, how much ground it covers. The year walked it room by room: the adab of speech, of eating, of guests, of travel, of sleep, of learning, of the road, of the market, of parents, neighbors and children, of animals and of the earth. A single hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari holds three of them in one breath, in paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or keep silent, let him honor his neighbor, let him honor his guest. Third, where the year traced it from. In a report in Malik's Muwatta, in paraphrase, the Prophet says he was sent to perfect good character. So adab is not an extra laid on top of the faith. That report puts it inside the reason the message came. Fourth, back to the boy. Notice what made it stick. The instructions were small enough to keep. Nobody handed him a book of rules. He got three things he could do at the very next meal, and he kept doing them from then on. That is how adab works across a whole life: one small courtesy, kept, until it is simply who you are at the table.
screen: `COURTESY TO ALLAH, PEOPLE, THINGS.` · `SPEECH, GUESTS, ROADS, ANIMALS…` · `SENT TO PERFECT CHARACTER.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: The practice: practice one adab. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Let the year's rooms pass by slowly: speech, the table, guests, the road, parents, neighbors, animals. Stop at the one that is nearest to your day today. Now make it as small as the boy's instructions. Not something huge, like being kinder to everyone. Something like: say bismillah before lunch, or let the other driver in, or return every greeting. Choose one. Hold it for the rest of the sit, as if you were tucking it in a pocket. The bell holds the time.
The manners. Adab: courtesy toward Allah, people and things, carried into the smallest moments of the day. Today's word.

Your line: courtesy. Today, keep the one small adab you chose, at least once, on purpose, the way the boy kept his at the very next meal. Tomorrow, the life cycle, reviewed. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Muslims learn adab from the Prophet's example in hadith: saying bismillah and eating with the right hand, greeting others, honoring guests and neighbors, and speaking well or staying silent, and teach them to children at the family table.
